book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo

chapters.relation: The Bock brothers ask whether Shawn's fake-psychic lie is morally permissible, testing it against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibitions on lying, Nietzsche's claim that all language is metaphorical (the 'Lights, Camera . . . Homicidio' acting-as-lying scene), and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means deception from The Prince. Using Sissela Bok's three-question test they contrast justified police undercover work - Juliet infiltrating the sorority in 'Scary Sherry' and the roller derby team in 'Talk Derby to Me' - with Shawn's ruse, which fails because it protects Shawn's own interests rather than others. They end by weighing Sorensen's bald-faced lies (Shawn's 'I know you know I'm not telling the truth') and conclude Chief Vick's genuine belief shows these are real, indefensible lies.

Ronda Bowen argues that because Shawn delivers true conclusions under a false justification (psychic power), the SBPD's beliefs are Gettier-style justified true beliefs rather than knowledge, using Plato's Theaetetus (perception and true judgment fail as definitions) as the frame and Gettier's Smith/Jones and Ford/Brown cases to model episodes like 'Spellingg Bee,' where the police infer Miklous's guilt from Shawn's staged psychic demonstration. John Hawthorne's lottery propositions explain why Lassiter's 'Shawn isn't a psychic' certainty can never be fully justified, and the chapter closes on internalism versus externalism and the reliability of testimony, concluding the detectives become internally justified only when they re-derive Shawn's conclusions through their own reasoning.

Amanda Lusky argues Shawn is a model pragmatist in the lineage of Peirce, James, and Dewey: he treats ideas as tools judged by consequences, is tough-minded about facts over theory (James's temperament distinction), and applies the pragmatic maxim from the squirrel-and-tree dispute to his loosely formed but working hunches. His co-operative inquiry with Gus and the SBPD - Gus's safe-cracking knowledge in 'Sixty Five Million Years Off,' passing Lassiter's polygraph in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' - enacts Dewey's democratic community solving problems together, and the chapter reads his tolerance of Gus's paranormal leads ('The Devil's in the Details') as pragmatic openness that enriches Santa Barbara's democratic life.

Courtland Lewis replays Plato's Theaetetus with Shawn and Henry to show that perception and true judgment fail as accounts of knowledge, then recasts both Gettier cases with Psych material: Chief Vick's justified-but-lucky belief about the chief-of-police job, and Juliet's disjunction 'Shawn is a psychic or Gus is in Mazatlan.' Since justified true belief is not knowledge, he argues Shawn's trained senses fit reliabilism - distinguished from lucky predictors like Leonard Koppett and probed through Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp against Gus's super sniffer - and closes by combining reliabilist-foundationalism (Alston's two levels of knowledge), coherence theory, and Klein's infinitism into Shawn's observe-eliminate-conclude method.

Dena Hurst reads Shawn as the mythological trickster - the fool who fools fools - who brings disorder to order by overturning hierarchies (Henry's ring-in-the-box lesson in '9 Lives'), taunting Lassiter, and inventing Gus's nicknames, while using his convenient psychic act to surface clues when found and excuse blunders. She argues people buy the act because we crave patterns and motivated narratives (Alfred Mele's work on seeing what we want to see), and closes with Hume's and Dennett's view that the self is a loose narrative we star in: Shawn literally invents himself as psychic detective, an exaggeration of the identities we all construct.

Courtney Neal explains that Santa Barbara believes Shawn is psychic because pseudoscience offers easier, more appealing explanations than the truth: in the pilot, 'he's psychic' beats 'he's the killer' as a narrative that fits the facts, and psychic claims are worded so they cannot be disproved. She shows how Shawn's real observational deductions are packaged through cold reading (the comic-convention scene in 'Shawn vs. the Red Phantom'), Robert Cialdini's social-influence principles of liking, social proof, and commitment/consistency, and the self-fulfilling prophecy of his reputation - so even Lassiter's skepticism cannot dislodge a belief the city keeps confirming.

Jeff Ewing applies Marx's critique of religion - the supernatural as ruling-class ideology, 'the opium of the people,' behind which priests and shamans hide real material processes and prop up hierarchy - to Shawn, who likewise masks his genuinely material observational talent as psychic gift to escape arrest in the pilot and keep access to SBPD cases. But the comparison inverts: unlike Marx's priests, Shawn serves ordinary people rather than the ruling class, and the chapter concludes he is better understood as an alienated worker - forced by a repressive state's threat of prosecution to sell a false product, defined by what he is not, and never credited for his true skill.

John Thompson argues Psych embodies the Daoist Way of reversal from the Daodejing and Zhuangzi: every episode begins with a death that triggers Shawn and Gus's irreverent, backwards-tracing investigation, their untrained spontaneous 'gifts' exemplify wu wei like Cook Ding carving an ox, and their bickering partnership is yin-yang interplay (as when Gus leads the joking in 'An Evening with Mr. Yang'). Zhuangzi singing at his wife's funeral parallels the Shabby the Sea Lion and 'Dust in the Wind' funeral parodies, the show's blurred TV-versus-fandom reality echoes the butterfly dream, Lassiter succeeds when he relaxes into wu wei ('Feet Don't Kill Me Now'), and the closing bloopers enact Dao's endless reversal - though the chapter ends by conceding Dao defies the very label 'Daoist show.'

Patricia Brace maps Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics categories of friendship onto Psych: Shawn's first-season ties to the SBPD are friendships of utility, the shared hobbies and bar nights (tap dancing in 'Feet Don't Kill Me Now,' 'Neil Simon's Lover's Retreat') build friendships of pleasure, and Shawn-Juliet matures from utilitarian boundaries into erotic friendship. Lassiter's lie-detector threat to protect Juliet in 'Shawn Rescues Darth Vader' and the lifelong Shawn-Gus bond ('Gus Walks into a Bank') approach complete friendship grounded in virtue, while the Henry-Shawn paternal friendship heals as Shawn develops the golden mean, and the vicious Mr. Yin and Yang - full of regret, incapable of complete friendship - show the life without it.

C. Scott Sevier argues Henry deliberately recreated Shawn as Aristotle's 'another self' - Lassiter's 'which one?' joke in the kidnapping episode makes the identity explicit - and reads this through Plato's Symposium: via Diotima's ladder of love and the doctrine of forms, Henry achieves immortality by reproducing beauty in his son's educated soul, not just his body. The chapter then frames Shawn's fierce independence against his constant recourse to Henry's voice as the collision between medieval deference to authority and the modern ideal of autonomy in Descartes and Kant, showing that both thinkers quietly borrowed from Augustine (the causal adequacy principle, the good will), so Shawn's 'autonomy' is itself the product of his father's training - an internalized authority indistinguishable from his own.

Mona Rocha asks whether Psych is sexist given Shawn's eighth-grade-girl caricature of Juliet in 'Spellingg Bee' and the secret knowledge kept from the show's women, then argues it is not: the women's inferior epistemic position is a byproduct of the con, not misogynist gatekeeping, because Shawn works collaboratively and non-hierarchically, shares credit (solving Lassiter's Back Bay Killer case for him in 'From the Earth to Starbucks'), gives the Chief the glory in 'There Might Be Blood,' and confronts the oilrig chauvinist outright. The contrast is The Mentalist, where Patrick Jane's withholding of deductions from Lisbon - going behind her back in 'Red Hair and Silver Tape' and getting evidence thrown out in 'Blood Money' - enacts patriarchal paternalism that undermines female leadership.

This chapter is a skeptical debunking tour of real-life 'psycho psychics' - Babylonian astrologers, the Delphi oracle that set Socrates testing the claim he was wisest, Nostradamus's hindsight-friendly quatrains, Blavatsky, Cayce, spoon-bender Uri Geller, and Sylvia Browne's failed Shawn Hornbeck prediction - arguing that no repeatable, peer-reviewed evidence of ESP has ever existed and that figures like cold-reading psychic detective Peter Hurkos thrive on gullibility. It ties to Psych through Gus's credulity about UFOs and werewolves and the real police practice of consulting psychic detectives that Shawn's con parodies, while Houdini's congressional testimony and James Randi's Million Dollar Challenge model the evidence-demanding skepticism the show's fake psychic gets away from.

holes.name: The Trickster Archetype
holes.what: A cross-cultural mythological figure who breaks rules, deceives, and disrupts established order, exposing conventions and opening new possibilities through mischief.
holes.why: Chapter 32's entire argument is that Shawn is a trickster - the fool who fools fools - and no taxonomy slug covers this mythological role.
